teaser: Nine people, one dog, and a painter who seems to be painting you.
review_notes:
The 1734 Alcázar fire damage: the infanta's left cheek is usually said to have been repainted afterwards by Juan García de Miranda; the lesson only says the canvas was damaged and trimmed at the edges (trimming is the common account, verify).
Cross of Santiago: knighthood granted in 1659; the story that Philip IV painted the cross himself is presented as a legend.
Picasso's 1957 series is given as 58 canvases (the full series in the Museu Picasso, Barcelona, including the pigeons and landscapes).
The title 'Las Meninas' first appearing in the Prado catalog of 1843.
Dimensions given as about 318 x 276 cm.
Identification of the man in the doorway as José Nieto, the queen's chamberlain, and of the dwarfs as Maribárbola and Nicolasito Pertusato follows Palomino (1724).

lesson.text: Count the people in this room who are staring straight at you. The painter is. The little girl in white is. So is the woman in the dark dress on the right. Now the uncomfortable question: why would a Spanish court of 1656 be looking at you?

The room is real. It was a long gallery in the Alcázar, the royal palace in Madrid, where Diego Velázquez had his studio. He was 57, painter to King Philip IV for more than thirty years. And he has put himself in the picture, brush in hand, behind a canvas so tall we only see its back.
Two people in this painting are not standing in the room with the others. Tap where you think they are.

spots.title: The mirror
spots.text: On the back wall, one frame glows while the paintings around it stay dark. It is a mirror. In it, under a red curtain, are the faint heads of King Philip IV and Queen Mariana.

lesson.text: If the king and queen appear in a mirror facing us, they must be standing where we stand. That solves the puzzle, and opens three more. Is Velázquez painting their portrait? Does the mirror reflect them, or the canvas he is working on? Have they just walked in to interrupt? The painting never says.
Las Meninas puts the most important people outside the picture, in your place. You are not looking at a scene. You are standing in it.

For almost two centuries the picture had no poetic name. Palace inventories called it “The Family of Philip IV.” The title Las Meninas only appeared in a Prado catalog of 1843. A menina was a young noblewoman who served a royal child.

The girl at the center is the Infanta Margarita, five years old, the king's daughter. Everyone around her has a job at court, and Velázquez knew each of them by name. What makes the group feel alive is that no two of them are doing the same thing with their eyes.

lesson.title: Four ways of looking
lesson.text: Follow the glances across the room, from the painter to the far door.

spots.title: The painter
spots.text: Velázquez leans back from his canvas, brush paused. It is the look of someone comparing a model with what he has painted so far. The model is wherever you are.

spots.title: The infanta
spots.text: Her head turns to the left but her eyes slide back toward us, as children do when something more interesting enters a room.

spots.title: Maribárbola
spots.text: A court dwarf from Germany, in dark blue. She faces us squarely and without ceremony, the steadiest gaze in the whole picture.

spots.title: The man on the stairs
spots.text: In the bright doorway, José Nieto, the queen's chamberlain, stops on the steps and looks back. He is the only one who can see everything: the room, the canvas and the royal couple.

lesson.text: Some have noticed, some have not yet. The maid kneeling on the left is still busy with the infanta. The boy on the far right is teasing the dog with his foot. That mix is why the scene feels like one second caught in mid-air, two hundred years before the first camera.

There is ambition behind the charm. In Spain, painting was still taxed and treated as a manual trade, like carpentry. Velázquez wanted it recognized as a noble art, and himself as a nobleman. So he shows the painter thinking rather than working, at home among royalty, as tall as anyone in the room.

The red cross on Velázquez's chest is the badge of the Order of Santiago, a knighthood he received only in 1659, three years after the painting was finished. It was added later. A legend says the king painted it on himself.
Now forget the people and consider how the canvas is divided. For a group portrait, it is built in a strange way: a great deal of it contains nobody at all.
Three lines show how the room is organized.

lines.label: The empty half
lines.text: Everything above this line is ceiling, shadow and dim paintings. All eleven figures live in the lower half. The dark space above them is what makes the room feel so high and so quiet.

lines.label: A wave of heads
lines.text: Join the heads from the painter to the boy and you get a line that dips, rises and dips again. Nobody is lined up as in an official portrait.

lines.label: Light from the right
lines.text: Daylight enters from a window on the right that we cannot see. It lands hardest on the infanta's pale hair and dress, so she shines without needing to be the largest figure.

lesson.text: A second light comes from the open door at the back, far behind everyone. Between those two lights, Velázquez paints something very hard to paint: the air itself. Figures get softer and grayer the deeper they stand, exactly as they would in a long, dusty room.

He does it with astonishingly little. From across the gallery in Madrid the silks look sewn and starched. Walk up to the canvas, which is about 3.2 meters tall (over 10 feet), and the dresses turn into loose flicks and smears of paint. The detail is made in your eye, not on the surface.

spots.title: The red cross
spots.text: The Cross of Santiago, painted onto the black doublet some years after the rest.

spots.title: A cup of water
spots.text: The kneeling menina, María Agustina Sarmiento, offers the infanta a small red clay jug on a tray. Scented clay cups like this were a fashionable way to drink cool water.

spots.title: The hidden canvas
spots.text: We see only the wooden stretcher and the raw back of the cloth. It is roughly as tall as Las Meninas itself, which has made many people wonder whether this is the picture he is painting.

spots.title: The mastiff
spots.text: A big, sleepy Spanish mastiff, patient under the boy's foot. Its fur is brushed in with a few broad, dry strokes.

spots.title: Nicolasito
spots.text: Nicolasito Pertusato, a young Italian dwarf at court, nudges the dog. His is the only real movement in the room.

spots.title: Two in the shadows
spots.text: A chaperone in a widow's white headdress speaks to a guard who is barely there, his face left as a blur. Velázquez lets the half-light swallow them.

spots.title: The second menina
spots.text: Isabel de Velasco begins a curtsy. Her body bends toward the infanta, but her eyes have already gone to the visitors.

lesson.text: On Christmas Eve 1734 the Alcázar burned down. Hundreds of paintings were lost. Las Meninas was rescued, damaged and later trimmed at the edges. The palace it shows no longer exists: the Royal Palace of Madrid stands on its site.

Painters have been circling this canvas ever since. The Italian Luca Giordano, seeing it a generation later, called it “the theology of painting,” the highest thing the art could do. In 1957 Picasso shut himself away for months and painted 58 variations on it, pulling it apart figure by figure.

Velázquez died in 1660, four years after finishing it, and left no explanation. So the first question still stands. When you face Las Meninas, are you the king, the queen, a visitor at the door, or simply the next person the painter has decided to study?

quiz.question: Who appears in the mirror on the back wall?
options: King Philip IV and Queen Mariana
quiz.explanation: The glowing frame is a mirror showing the royal couple, who must be standing where the viewer stands.

quiz.question: What did the word “menina” mean at the Spanish court?
options: A young noblewoman serving a royal child
A princess who would inherit the throne
quiz.explanation: Meninas were young ladies-in-waiting, like the two attending the infanta.

quiz.question: Why is the red cross on the painter's chest surprising?
options: It is the wrong color for his order
He received that knighthood three years after finishing the picture
quiz.explanation: He joined the Order of Santiago in 1659, so the cross was added later.

quiz.question: How is the upper half of the canvas used?
options: It is almost empty: ceiling, shadow and dim paintings
It shows a second row of courtiers
quiz.explanation: All the figures are in the lower half, and the dark space above makes the room feel tall and quiet.

quiz.question: What did Picasso do with Las Meninas in 1957?
options: He restored it for the Prado
He bought a copy of it
quiz.explanation: He spent months reworking the composition in a series of 58 canvases.

facts.text: The painting has been called Las Meninas ever since Velázquez finished it.
facts.explanation: It was listed as “The Family of Philip IV” and only got its current title in 1843.

facts.text: Las Meninas survived the fire that destroyed the palace where it was painted.
facts.explanation: It was rescued when the Alcázar of Madrid burned in 1734.

facts.text: The main light in the scene comes from a chandelier in the ceiling.
facts.explanation: Daylight comes from an unseen window on the right, with a second light from the door at the back.
